title: 50. Numeracy & Number Systems: Locating Square Roots Between Integers
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.concept: Locating a Square Root Between Consecutive Integers
questions.learningObjective: Locate the square root of a non-perfect-square integer between two consecutive integers.
questions.question: Between which two consecutive integers does \(\sqrt{10}\) lie?
questions.explanation: The nearby perfect squares are \(3^2=9\) and \(4^2=16\). Since \(9<10<16\), taking square roots gives \(3<\sqrt{10}<4\). Therefore, \(\sqrt{10}\) lies between \(3\) and \(4\).
questions.hint: Find the two consecutive perfect squares that surround the radicand.

questions.concept: Locating a Square Root Using Perfect Squares
questions.learningObjective: Use neighboring perfect squares to locate a square root between consecutive integers.
questions.question: Between which two consecutive integers does \(\sqrt{26}\) lie?
questions.explanation: Since \(5^2=25\) and \(6^2=36\), we have \(25<26<36\). Therefore, \(5<\sqrt{26}<6\), so \(\sqrt{26}\) lies between \(5\) and \(6\).
questions.hint: Compare the radicand with the squares of nearby consecutive integers.

questions.concept: Locating a Square Root Near a Perfect Square
questions.learningObjective: Locate a square root by identifying the closest consecutive perfect-square bounds.
questions.question: Between which two consecutive integers does \(\sqrt{80}\) lie?
questions.explanation: The consecutive perfect squares around \(80\) are \(8^2=64\) and \(9^2=81\). Since \(64<80<81\), it follows that \(8<\sqrt{80}<9\). Therefore, \(\sqrt{80}\) lies between \(8\) and \(9\).
questions.hint: Look for the perfect square immediately below and immediately above the radicand.

questions.concept: Identifying Consecutive Integer Bounds for a Square Root
questions.learningObjective: Determine the consecutive integer interval containing a given square root.
questions.question: Which interval correctly contains \(\sqrt{45}\)?
questions.explanation: We have \(6^2=36\) and \(7^2=49\). Because \(36<45<49\), taking square roots gives \(6<\sqrt{45}<7\). Therefore, the correct interval is \(6<\sqrt{45}<7\).
questions.hint: Square the consecutive integers in each proposed interval and compare those squares with \(45\).

questions.concept: Greatest Integer Below a Square Root
questions.learningObjective: Use consecutive perfect-square bounds to identify the greatest integer less than a square root.
questions.question: What is the greatest integer less than \(\sqrt{50}\)?
questions.explanation: Since \(7^2=49\) and \(8^2=64\), we have \(49<50<64\). Thus, \(7<\sqrt{50}<8\). Therefore, the greatest integer less than \(\sqrt{50}\) is \(7\).
questions.hint: First locate the square root between two consecutive integers, then identify the integer immediately to its left.

questions.learningObjective: Verify the correct consecutive integer bounds for a square root using squared endpoints.
questions.question: Which inequality correctly locates \(\sqrt{115}\)?
questions.explanation: The relevant perfect squares are \(10^2=100\) and \(11^2=121\). Since \(100<115<121\), taking square roots gives \(10<\sqrt{115}<11\). Therefore, \(10<\sqrt{115}<11\) correctly locates \(\sqrt{115}\).
questions.hint: Compare \(115\) with the squares of the integer endpoints in each option.

questions.concept: Reverse Reasoning from Square Root Bounds
questions.learningObjective: Determine which radicand produces a square root within a specified interval.
questions.question: Which value of \(n\) makes \(12<\sqrt{n}<13\)?
questions.explanation: Square the interval endpoints: \(12^2=144\) and \(13^2=169\). The condition \(12<\sqrt{n}<13\) is equivalent to \(144<n<169\). The value \(150\) satisfies this condition, while \(170\) is greater than \(169\). Therefore, \(n=150\).
questions.hint: Square both integer bounds to determine the required range for the radicand.

questions.concept: Selecting a Square Root from a Given Integer Interval
questions.learningObjective: Identify which square root lies within a specified pair of consecutive integers.
questions.question: Which square root lies between \(4\) and \(5\)?
questions.explanation: Numbers whose square roots lie between \(4\) and \(5\) must have radicands between \(4^2=16\) and \(5^2=25\). Since \(16<23<25\), \(\sqrt{23}\) lies between \(4\) and \(5\). Since \(26>25\), \(\sqrt{26}>5\). Therefore, \(\sqrt{23}\) is correct.
questions.hint: Translate the interval for the square root into an interval for the radicand by squaring the endpoints.

questions.concept: Locating Multiple Square Roots in the Same Integer Interval
questions.learningObjective: Identify the pair of consecutive integers between which two given square roots both lie.
questions.question: Both \(\sqrt{200}\) and \(\sqrt{220}\) lie between the same two consecutive integers. Which pair is it?
questions.explanation: The relevant consecutive perfect squares are \(14^2=196\) and \(15^2=225\). Both radicands satisfy \(196<200<225\) and \(196<220<225\). Therefore, \(14<\sqrt{200}<15\) and \(14<\sqrt{220}<15\), so both square roots lie between \(14\) and \(15\).
questions.hint: Find one pair of consecutive perfect squares that contains both radicands.

questions.concept: Generalizing Square Root Bounds for Integer Radicands
questions.learningObjective: Determine the complete integer range of radicands whose square roots lie between two consecutive integers.
questions.question: Suppose \(n\) is an integer and \(9<\sqrt{n}<10\). Which statement gives all possible integer values of \(n\)?
questions.explanation: Squaring the positive bounds gives \(81<n<100\). Because \(n\) is an integer, the smallest possible value is \(82\) and the largest possible value is \(99\). Therefore, all possible integer values satisfy \(82\le n\le 99\).
questions.hint: Square the strict inequalities first, then use the fact that \(n\) must be an integer.
